author: Epiphanius of Salamis
occasion: The work is offered as a handbook for those who wish to gain broad learning about the parts of the divine Scriptures, specifically concerning measures and weights.
argument: Epiphanius invites readers who desire fuller knowledge of the divine Scriptures to use this handbook on measures and weights. He first states that the student of letters must know how many parts there are in the prophecies. He says the prophecies are divided into ten kinds of contemplation, but the source lists only nine items: teachings, contemplations, exhortations, threats, lamentations, dirges, prayers, histories, and predictions. Alongside these prophecies he lists five accompanying signs: the rejection of the former people, the rejection of the law according to the flesh, the New Covenant, the calling of the nations, and Christ.

outline.move: Epiphanius introduces the handbook on measures and weights, states that the prophecies are divided into ten kinds of contemplation but lists nine, and lists five accompanying signs.

_unresolved_facts.claim: He says the prophecies are divided into ten kinds of contemplation, but the source lists only nine items
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Εἰς δέκα γὰρ διῄρηνται θεωρίας αἱ προφητεῖαι, οὕτως περιέχουσαι· διδασκαλίας, θεωρίας, προτροπάς, ἀπειλάς, ὀλοφυρμούς, θρήνους, εὐχάς, ἱστορίας, προρρήσεις
_unresolved_facts.fix: The source states the prophecies are divided into ten kinds of contemplation (εἰς δέκα γὰρ διῄρηνται θεωρίας) but lists only nine items; the brief correctly notes this discrepancy but should not attribute the claim of 'ten' as Epiphanius's own assertion separate from what the text actually states—rather, the text itself claims ten but enumerates nine.

_unresolved_facts.claim: He first states that the student of letters must know how many parts there are in the prophecies
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Καὶ πρῶτον μὲν δεῖ εἰδέναι τὸν φιλολόγον, πόσα τυγχάνει ἐν ταῖς προφητείαις μέρη
_unresolved_facts.fix: He first states that the student of letters (φιλολόγον, 'lover of learning/letters') must know how many parts there are in the prophecies

_unresolved_facts.claim: Epiphanius invites readers who desire fuller knowledge of the divine Scriptures
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Εἴ τις δὲ θέλει τῶν ἐν ταῖς θείαις Γραφαῖς εἰδέναι τὰ πρὸς πολυπειρίαν μέρη
_unresolved_facts.fix: Epiphanius invites readers who desire to know the parts contributing to broad learning/experience (πολυπειρίαν) in the divine Scriptures
